title: SARAH GAVE HER SERVANT HAGAR TO ABRAHAM—Was This Adultery, Polygamy, Surrogacy, or Something Else?
paragraphs: SARAH GAVE HER SERVANT HAGAR TO ABRAHAM—Was This Adultery, Polygamy, Surrogacy, or Something Else?

Genesis 16 is not merely the disturbing story of a wife giving another woman to her husband. It is the story of what can happen when wounded people become so desperate for God’s promise that they try to manufacture with human hands what only God can give by grace.
There is one sentence in Genesis that becomes more uncomfortable the longer you stare at it.
“And Sarai Abram’s wife took Hagar her maid the Egyptian…and gave her to her husband Abram to be his wife.”
Not merely his servant.
Not merely a woman who would carry a baby.
The Hebrew text says:
וַתִּקַּח שָׂרַי אֵשֶׁת־אַבְרָם אֶת־הָגָר הַמִּצְרִית שִׁפְחָתָהּ… וַתִּתֵּן אֹתָהּ לְאַבְרָם אִישָׁהּ לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה
Vattiqqaḥ Sarai eshet-Avram et-Hagar hammitzrit shifḥatah… vattitten otah le-Avram ishah lo le-ishshah.
In plain sense:
“Sarai, Abram’s wife, took Hagar the Egyptian, her female servant…and gave her to Abram her husband, to him as a wife.”
That last Hebrew expression matters:
לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה — lo le’ishshah — “to him as a wife.”
Genesis actually calls Hagar a wife in this scene. Many major English translations likewise render Genesis 16:3 as Sarai giving Hagar to Abram “as a wife” or “to be his wife.”
And suddenly the question becomes much harder.
Was Abraham committing adultery?
Was this polygamy?
Was Hagar functioning as an ancient surrogate?
Was she a concubine?
And perhaps the question that should disturb us most:
Why would Sarah ever agree to this?
Before judging her from the safety of thousands of years later, sit in her tent for a moment.
She had heard the promise.
She had followed her husband away from familiarity.
She had watched years disappear.
Month after month.
Year after year.
Still no child.
No pregnancy.
No son.
No visible fulfillment.
God had promised Abram descendants, yet Sarai’s body seemed to be preaching the opposite sermon.
Imagine living between those two realities.
God says promise.
Your circumstances say impossible.
God says wait.
Your biological clock says time is running out.
God says trust Me.
Your pain whispers, “Maybe God needs your help.”
That is where Genesis 16 begins.
Not primarily with lust.
With impatience.
Not with two strangers meeting in secret.
With a husband and wife trying to solve a problem that apparently refused to move.
And that makes this chapter frighteningly relatable.
Because you may never give your servant to your spouse, but you may know exactly what it feels like to become tired of waiting on God.
You prayed.
Nothing changed.
You believed.
Nothing happened.
You watched somebody else receive the thing you had begged God for.
Another wedding.
Another pregnancy.
Another healing testimony.
Another promotion.
Another restored marriage.
Another answered prayer.
And eventually faith becomes exhausted enough to start negotiating with desperation.
Maybe I need to make something happen.
Maybe I misunderstood God.
Maybe this shortcut is acceptable because my intentions are good.
Maybe God promised the destination and does not particularly care how I get there.
That is the dangerous heartbeat beneath Genesis 16.
Sarai tells Abram:
“Behold now, the LORD hath restrained me from bearing: I pray thee, go in unto my maid; it may be that I may obtain children by her.”
Then comes a sentence almost painfully understated:
“And Abram hearkened to the voice of Sarai.”
He agreed.
And here the narrator uses language that should make careful readers of Genesis uncomfortable.
Sarai took Hagar.
Then she gave her to Abram.
“Took.”
“Gave.”
Those verbs echo an earlier catastrophe in Genesis, where the woman “took” the forbidden fruit and “gave” it to her husband, who ate.

Genesis 16 is not identical to Genesis 3, and we should not force every verbal similarity into an allegory. But the narrative resemblance is difficult to miss: human beings encounter a situation in which trusting God is required, then take matters into their own hands.
And Abram, like Adam before him, listens and participates.
So was this adultery?
If by “adultery” we mean Abram secretly having sexual relations with a woman who was not recognized as his wife, Genesis 16 does not describe the event that way.
The Hebrew text explicitly says Hagar was given to Abram לְאִשָּׁה — le’ishshah — “as a wife.”
That makes simply calling the episode “an affair” misleading.
But neither should we swing to the opposite extreme and conclude that because Genesis reports this arrangement, God therefore approved it.
The Bible often describes human behavior without prescribing it.
That distinction matters enormously.
Scripture records murder without endorsing murder.
It records deception without sanctifying deception.
It records polygamous households without presenting their dysfunction as God’s ideal.
And Genesis has already established its foundational marriage pattern before Abraham ever appears.
Genesis 2:24 describes a man leaving father and mother, being joined to his wife, and the two becoming “one flesh.”
Jesus Himself later reaches back past centuries of broken human arrangements to this creation text when teaching about marriage.
The existence of polygamy in biblical history therefore does not automatically equal divine endorsement of polygamy.
So what happened in Genesis 16?

The most textually responsible description is that Hagar entered a secondary marital arrangement within Abram’s household, an arrangement connected directly to Sarai’s desire to obtain offspring through her servant. Calling it a form of ancient surrogate arrangement can help modern readers understand its reproductive purpose, but “surrogacy” must be used cautiously because modern surrogacy is not socially or legally identical to what Genesis describes.
Calling Hagar merely a “surrogate,” however, can hide something the Hebrew text refuses to let us forget:
Hagar was a person.
A woman.
An Egyptian servant under Sarai’s authority.
And now her body had become the place where an entire household tried to solve its crisis.
She conceives.
Immediately everything changes.
The solution becomes another wound.
Hagar sees that she is pregnant, and Sarai becomes diminished in her eyes.
Sarai feels dishonored.
She turns toward Abram:
“My wrong be upon thee.”
The plan that was supposed to heal her pain has multiplied it.
That is what shortcuts so often do.
They promise relief without revealing the interest rate.
You wanted companionship so badly that you ignored what you knew about the relationship.
You wanted financial security so desperately that compromise started looking reasonable.
You wanted recognition so badly that your private character became negotiable.
You wanted the prayer answered so urgently that you stopped asking whether the method honored the God you were asking to bless it.
Then eventually you wake up surrounded by consequences and whisper:
How did I get here?
Genesis 16 answers:
Sometimes slowly.
Sometimes reasonably.
Sometimes through decisions that initially sounded practical.
Sarai blames Abram.
Abram hands responsibility for Hagar back to Sarai.
Sarai deals harshly with Hagar.
And Hagar runs.
The pregnant servant disappears into the wilderness.
Think about that.
The woman who was used as the household’s solution has now become its refugee.
She is pregnant.
Alone.
Vulnerable.
Away from home.
Away from security.
Away from the people whose choices helped put her there.
And this is where the story suddenly becomes breathtaking.
Because humanity may lose sight of Hagar.
God does not.
“The angel of the LORD found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness.”
Found her.
Do not rush past those words.
God found her.
Hagar did not have Abraham’s social position.
She did not have Sarah’s authority.
She was Egyptian.
A servant.
Pregnant.
Running.
Yet heaven knew exactly where she was.
God addresses her personally:
“Hagar…”
He knows her name.
Then comes one of the most extraordinary moments in Genesis.
Hagar responds to the God who speaks to her by saying:
אַתָּה אֵל רֳאִי — Attah El Ro’i
Commonly understood as:
“You are a God who sees me.”
The woman who had been treated as somebody else’s means to an end discovers that she is not invisible to God.
Read that again if you have ever felt used.
If someone benefited from you and discarded you…
God sees.
If your family knows the version of the story that protects everyone except you…
God sees.
If you have cried where nobody could hear you…
God sees.
If people reduced you to your failure, your usefulness, your past, your body, your status, your mistake, your addiction, your divorce, your shame…
God sees.
And He sees more than what happened to you.
He sees what is happening inside you.
This does not mean every action Hagar takes is automatically righteous, any more than every action Abraham or Sarah takes is righteous.
Genesis is brutally honest about broken people.
That honesty is part of its beauty.
The Bible does not need to airbrush its heroes.
Abraham can be the man of faith and still make disastrous decisions.
Sarah can receive an extraordinary promise and still act out of fear and desperation.
Hagar can suffer injustice and still become entangled in human conflict.
Nobody in Genesis 16 needs cosmetic editing.
And that is exactly why this story prepares our hearts to understand grace.
Because Scripture is not ultimately the story of flawless human beings climbing toward God.
It is the story of the holy God pursuing fallen human beings who cannot save themselves.
Abraham could not manufacture the covenant promise.
Sarah could not engineer it.
Hagar could not control the storm around her.
God would have to remain faithful.
And He did.
The promised covenant son would eventually come through Sarah exactly as God determined.
Isaac would not be the trophy of successful human manipulation.
He would be the child of promise.
Yet God did not therefore treat Ishmael as worthless.
He heard.
He saw.
He cared.
Even his name carries that testimony.
יִשְׁמָעֵאל — Yishma’el — Ishmael
“God hears.”
A woman who discovered that God sees her would give birth to a son whose name proclaimed that God hears.
Seen.
Heard.
In the wilderness.
Maybe somebody reading this needs those two truths more than another theological argument.
You are seen.
You are heard.
But Genesis 16 is still not the end.
Not even close.
Because Abraham’s family story keeps moving toward something greater than Abraham.
Through Isaac comes Jacob.
Through Jacob comes Israel.
Through Israel comes Judah.
And through that covenant history, in the fullness of time, comes Jesus Christ.
Jesus enters a human family line filled with scandal, weakness, sexual brokenness, deception, rivalry, outsiders, sinners, failures, and astonishing mercy.
The Gospel does not say that our sins were harmless.
It says something infinitely better:
Our sins can be forgiven.
Jesus did not come to tell broken people how to become impressive enough for God.
He came because we could never repair the breach ourselves.
At the cross, Christ bore sin.
He carried judgment.
He died.
And He rose.
What Abraham and Sarah could not do by human effort becomes a recurring biblical lesson: what God promises ultimately depends upon God’s faithfulness.
And salvation brings that truth to its highest point.
You cannot engineer your own redemption.
You cannot sleep with the right Hagar, construct the right plan, perform enough religion, give enough money, clean yourself up enough, or hide your past deeply enough to manufacture salvation.
You need Jesus.
Maybe your “Hagar” is not a person.
Maybe it is the thing you created because you became tired of waiting.
The relationship you forced.
The lie you maintained.
The compromise you rationalized.
The secret habit you use to numb yourself.
The identity you manufactured because you feared the person God was calling you to become.
Maybe your life currently contains consequences from decisions you wish you could reverse.
Listen carefully.
Repentance does not mean pretending those consequences never happened.
Grace does not call evil good.
Forgiveness does not rewrite history by lying about history.
Jesus does something far more powerful.
He redeems sinners inside real history.
He takes people with chapters they would rather tear out and gives them a future those chapters could never have predicted.
That is why the Gospel is not self-improvement.
It is resurrection.
So before you leave Genesis 16 arguing about whether Hagar should technically be called a wife, concubine, secondary wife, or surrogate, allow the text to ask something much closer to your heart:
Where have you become so tired of trusting God that you are tempted to manufacture what you believe He owes you?
Be honest.
Maybe this hit harder than you expected.
Maybe underneath all your Christian vocabulary you have been angry with God.
Maybe you are tired of waiting.
Maybe everybody thinks you are strong, but privately you are exhausted.
Maybe you made your own Genesis 16 decision and now you are living inside the consequences.
Do not hide from Christ.
Bring it into the light.
Confess it.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive the mercy you cannot earn.
Jesus is not frightened by the chapter you are ashamed to show Him.
Your comment may become the sentence another wounded believer sees and realizes, “I’m not the only one.”
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somebody on your Facebook friends list may be quietly living in their own wilderness.
Send it privately to the person whose name came into your mind while reading.
Send it even to the skeptic who thinks Christianity is a religion built on pretending religious people have perfect families. Genesis itself destroys that illusion.
There may come a night when you need to read again that El Ro’i sees you.
But voluntary generosity can be an act of worship when it comes from a willing heart.
A share costs nothing, yet it may place the Gospel in front of someone we could never reach ourselves.
Because somewhere tonight there is another Sarah who is tired of waiting.
Another Abraham tempted to compromise.
Another Hagar running through a wilderness believing nobody sees.
Another believer ashamed of the mess created by yesterday’s decisions.
And another soul who desperately needs to discover that the God of Scripture does not abandon His redemptive purposes simply because human beings made a mess along the way.
Genesis 16 is scandalous.
But scandal does not get the final word.
Failure does not get the final word.
Your worst chapter does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
The wilderness may remember how you arrived there, but grace is already writing what happens after you are found.
